Content:
Whenever we have an expression that's written as a difference of squares, we can factor the expression by applying the difference of squares formula:
[MATH: a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)]

Content:
Factoring a difference of squares works even when the numbers involved are not perfect squares! The key is to recognize that any positive number can be written as the square of its square root, even if that square root is irrational.

Content:
Let’s illustrate this idea by factoring the following expression:
[MATH: x^2 - 2]

Content:
To factor this expression, we first note that the [MATH: 2] can be expressed as a square:
[MATH: 2 = \big(\sqrt{2}\big)^2]

Content:
This means we can write our expression [MATH: x^2-2] as a difference of squares:
[MATH: x^{2} − (sqrt(2))^{2}]

Content:
Finally, we factor the expression using the difference of squares formula with [MATH: a=x] and [MATH: b=\sqrt{2}{:}]

Content:
[MATH: x^{2} − (sqrt(2))^{2} = (x − sqrt(2))(x + sqrt(2))]

Then, we factor the expression using the difference of squares formula:

items.title: Factoring a Difference of Squares Whose Terms Have a Common Factor

sections.normalized_html: Factor the expression [MATH: \dfrac{4m^2}{5}-36.]
sections.readable_text: Factor the expression [MATH: \dfrac{4m^2}{5}-36.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The terms of our expression have a common factor of [MATH: 4.] So, we simplify the expression by factoring it out:

[MATH: \dfrac{4m^2}{5}-36 = 4\left(\dfrac{m^2}{5}-9\right)]

Now, let's factor the expression inside parentheses using the difference of squares formula:

[MATH: (m^{2})/(5) − 9|=; ((m)/(sqrt(5)))^{2} − 3^{2}|=; ((m)/(sqrt(5)) − 3)((m)/(sqrt(5)) + 3)]

Therefore, our original expression factors as follows:

[MATH: \dfrac{4m^2}{5}-36 = 4\left(\dfrac{m}{\sqrt5} - 3 \right)\left(\dfrac{m}{\sqrt5} + 3 \right)]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Whenever we have an expression that's written as a difference of squares, we can factor the expression by applying the difference of squares formula:
[MATH: a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)]

Content:
Factoring a difference of squares works even when the numbers involved are not perfect squares! The key is to recognize that any positive number can be written as the square of its square root, even if that square root is irrational.

Content:
Let’s illustrate this idea by factoring the following expression:
[MATH: x^2 - 2]

Content:
To factor this expression, we first note that the [MATH: 2] can be expressed as a square:
[MATH: 2 = \big(\sqrt{2}\big)^2]

Content:
This means we can write our expression [MATH: x^2-2] as a difference of squares:
[MATH: x^{2} − (sqrt(2))^{2}]

Content:
Finally, we factor the expression using the difference of squares formula with [MATH: a=x] and [MATH: b=\sqrt{2}{:}]

Content:
[MATH: x^{2} − (sqrt(2))^{2} = (x − sqrt(2))(x + sqrt(2))]
